Project 01 · GEOG 5530 Remote Sensing & Image Analysis

Identifying Urban Sprawl in Collin County, Texas (2015–2025)

Landsat 8 OLI · Supervised Maximum Likelihood Classification · Change Detection · ArcGIS Pro

Collin County ranked 2nd in the U.S. for single-year numeric population gain in 2024–2025, growing from 144,000 residents in 1990 to an estimated 1.3 million today. This study applies supervised maximum likelihood classification and unsupervised Iso Cluster methods to Landsat 8 imagery across two time points to quantify a decade of suburban land conversion — mapping where, how fast, and in what spatial pattern built-up land is replacing agricultural and natural cover across the county's full 2,296 km² extent.

Urban Change Detection Map — Collin County (2015–2025)
Orange = newly urbanized areas · 527 km² (22.97% of county) converted from non-built-up to built-up

Research Question

Where and at what rate is agricultural and natural land converting to urban impervious surface across one of America's fastest-growing counties?

Methods

Supervised MLC and unsupervised Iso Cluster on summer-season Landsat 8 composites; spectral index guidance (NDVI, NDWI, NDBI); stratified random accuracy assessment (60 pts); binary change detection via Reclassify + Combine.

Key Finding

Built-up land expanded from 472 km² (20.6%) to 988 km² (43.0%) — a net gain of 516 km² in one decade. Sprawl is multi-nodal and most intense around Celina, Prosper, Anna, and Frisco along major highway corridors.

Planning Relevance

Provides a reproducible remote sensing framework for stormwater, urban heat, and infrastructure planning as the county moves toward a projected 2.2M residents by 2050.

Project 02 · GEOG 5550 Advanced GIS

Assessing Transit Accessibility in the City of Denton, Texas

ArcGIS Pro · Near Tool · DCTA GTFS Data · ACS Demographics · Transit Equity Analysis

With Denton's population surging past 139,000 — driven by UNT and TWU enrollment and DFW suburbanization — the DCTA network serves a dense urban core while leaving much of the city's outer residential areas effectively unserved. This study classifies all 104 Census block groups into four accessibility tiers using Euclidean distance to the nearest DCTA stop, then cross-references findings with ACS zero-vehicle household and poverty data to identify where transit need and supply diverge most sharply — revealing a center-periphery equity gap with direct policy implications for DCTA's 2024 service restructuring.

Research Question

Are DCTA's 159 bus stops equitably distributed across Denton's block groups, and which communities face the greatest gap between transit need and supply?

Methods

Near Tool (Euclidean distance from block group centroid to nearest DCTA stop); Spatial Join for stop counts per BG; four-tier classification via Python code block in Field Calculator; ACS demographic overlay for zero-vehicle households and poverty.

Key Finding

Transit supply is heavily concentrated in a small urban core (median = 0 stops/BG, skewness = 2.89). Outer residential block groups with elevated zero-vehicle rates fall in the Transit Desert tier — transit-dependent but transit-poor.

Policy Relevance

Directly critiques DCTA's 2024 GoZone restructuring, which removed on-demand microtransit from Denton — precisely the service model suited to serve outer Transit Desert block groups identified in this analysis.
